documents.abstract: Abstract Video surveillance systems have witnessed rapid advancements over the past two decades, fueled by progress in computer vision, artificial intelligence, and edge computing. However, despite extensive research, there remains a need for a review that synthesizes the architectures, methodologies, and evolving trends of intelligent video surveillance systems from a system-level perspective. Most existing literature reviews focus narrowly on individual tasks such as object detection, motion tracking, or anomaly recognition, without addressing how these components integrate within a complete system. This paper addresses this gap by conducting a systematic review of research published between January 2000 and July 2025, drawing from major digital repositories. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) it proposes a structured taxonomy of intelligent surveillance systems based on key functionalities, including object detection, motion tracking, abnormal event detection, vehicle and traffic monitoring, object counting, and multi-camera coordination; (2) it provides a comparative analysis of methodologies, datasets, and platforms used across studies; and (3) it explores the interconnections among these core tasks while identifying critical challenges such as real-time processing, privacy preservation, data scalability, and system interoperability. Key outcomes of this review include the identification of underexplored research areas—such as federated learning and cross-camera integration—and practical guidelines for designing next-generation surveillance systems. The literature analyzed was sourced from major digital repositories including IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, arXiv, Springer, and the ACM Digital Library.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human societies. In the many attempts to capture the novel trend of AI entering in all aspects of human life these days, hardly any research covers sustainability aspects of AI encroaching society. In the teaching of sustainability, AI appears as an way to improve carbon footprint as for energy savings opportunities – for instance by using online resources instead of physical books, reducing cognitive load of tedious tasks that had to be performed in educational settings previously, such as sifting through many books to find applicable cases in law school etc. At the same time, AI may create enormous environmental costs – e.g., through its electricity consumption use for big data storage and analytics – but also sustainability challenges – e.g., through eternally-living algorithms and technical devices. This chapter proposes weighing the costs and benefits of AI in sustainability education. In a Law & Economics analysis, the advantages and disadvantages of AI in sustainability education will be compared in order to present a framework to harvest the benefits but prepare for coping with the downsides of AI in sustainability education. Future student learning experience enhancement and educational changes due to AI in the future will be prospectively anticipated in the discussion. The future of education may positively develop in less cognitive load and diligent learning-by-heart but shift towards creative solution finding, navigating through a digital online jungle and development social network skills to find the right tools in a growing ocean of mushrooming AI advancements.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The development of digital technology, artificial intelligence, environmental concerns, and changing workforce needs has encouraged organizations to adopt more sustainable approaches to talent management. This study aims to examine the development of sustainable talent management, identify its key practices, and analyze the role of digitalization, artificial intelligence, employee skill development, motivation, and retention in supporting organizational sustainability. This study employs a qualitative approach using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) based on the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Relevant studies were identified through systematic searches of selected databases, screened according to predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and analyzed using content analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that sustainable talent management has evolved from a short-term, performance-oriented approach toward a more strategic and long-term perspective that emphasizes organizational sustainability and employee development. Its key practices include talent attraction and selection, competency development, employee motivation, and retention, supported by digital technologies and artificial intelligence. However, the implementation of these technologies requires continuous employee skill development and a human-centered approach to ensure that technological advancement remains aligned with employee and organizational needs. The study concludes that sustainable talent management integrates technological, human, social, and environmental aspects to support organizational sustainability and long-term organizational resilience.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

documents.abstract: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS's pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question-answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22%-33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4%-22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.

Nepali-English code-switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code-switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two-stage synthetic-to-real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi-speaker, dual-engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross-domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (-1.88 pp) and switch-point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (-7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT-converged encoder-decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER-only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near-zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.

Code-switched (CS) automatic speech recognition (ASR) remains difficult because real CS speech is scarce and synthetic speech does not fully match it. We investigate whether synthetic CS speech is more useful for learning an adaptation-friendly initialization than for ordinary continual fine-tuning. We propose SyRA-CS, a pair-specific synthetic-to-real adaptation framework based on Reptile meta-learning. For each language pair and pretrained model, we meta-train on the corresponding synthetic CS-FLEURS subset and then adapt using one hour of labeled real target speech. We evaluate four architectural settings: Encoder-CTC, FastConformer-RNN-T, Attention Encoder-Decoder (AED) and Speech-LLM. Experiments cover on Arabic-, French-, German-, and Hindi-English, against synthetic-only transfer, real-only fine-tuning, and continual fine-tuning. SyRA-CS improves over continual fine-tuning on WER in all 16 model-pair comparisons and on CER in 15 of 16, with relative macro WER reductions of 17.7% for XLS-R and 5.3-5.8% for the other three models. The gains hold across the tested models but vary in size across architectures, language pairs and metrics.

Background: Nephron-sparing surgery has become a standard approach for localized renal masses because it preserves renal function while providing oncologic control comparable with radical nephrectomy. Robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) has expanded the minimally invasive management of increasingly complex renal tumors. This review summarizes contemporary clinical outcomes and emerging technologies in RAPN. Materials and Methods: A PRISMA-guided literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus for peer-reviewed English-language human studies published between January 2020 and June 2025. Search terms included robot-assisted partial nephrectomy, robotic partial nephrectomy, RAPN, nephron-sparing surgery, single-port robotics, augmented reality, three-dimensional surgical planning, fluorescence-guided nephrectomy, and learning curve. Manual reference screening was also performed. Twenty eligible studies were included for qualitative synthesis; quantitative meta-analysis was not performed because of heterogeneity in study designs and endpoints. Results: Comparative randomized, propensity-matched, and multicenter studies generally showed faster postoperative recovery, less pain, and shorter hospitalization with RAPN than with open partial nephrectomy, while maintaining comparable oncologic outcomes. RAPN was feasible for hilar, endophytic, and solitary-kidney tumors in experienced centers. Three-dimensional planning and augmented-reality guidance improved anatomical visualization and operative planning, while indocyanine-green near-infrared fluorescence supported selective ischemia and perfusion assessment. Single-port RAPN demonstrated broadly comparable perioperative outcomes with multiport approaches, although early adoption may involve longer operative times. Structured learning-curve and training models were associated with progressive improvement in operative performance and complication rates. Conclusion: Current evidence supports RAPN as a safe and effective nephron-sparing approach across a broad range of renal tumor complexity. Artificial intelligence-assisted image guidance, fluorescence-based perfusion assessment, three-dimensional planning, and next-generation single-port platforms may further improve precision and functional preservation. Larger multicenter randomized studies and longer follow-up are needed to establish durable oncologic, functional, and cost-effectiveness benchmarks.

The article substantiates theoretical and pedagogical foundations for developing students’ positive attitudes towards inclusive education and professional motivation. It explains the interrelationship of inclusive awareness, value acceptance, empathy, professional self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, practical experience and reflection. A staged methodology based on cases, simulations, service learning, microteaching and reflective portfolios is proposed.
topics: Inclusion and Disability in Education and Sport

documents.abstract: In their lead article in Frontiers in Science, Boeringer et al. propose targeting networks of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) as a promising strategy for geroprotection (Boeringer et al. 2026). This approach builds on the remarkable versatility of GPCRs, which sense a wide range of extracellular signals, engage diverse signaling pathways, are broadly expressed across tissues, and play important roles in many disease processes. By framing the GPCRome as a central, druggable regulator of multiple hallmarks of aging, from inflammaging and mitochondrial dysfunction to stem cell depletion, the authors advance an intriguing hypothesis in which systems pharmacology could be used to rebalance several of these processes simultaneously, potentially delaying the onset of chronic disease and extending healthspan. The proposed integration of artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and quantum computing to rationally manipulate such complex signaling networks is bold and thought-provoking.At the same time, translating this compelling vision into therapeutic reality presents formidable biophysical, computational, and experimental challenges. The authors explicitly acknowledge several of these limitations, including the sparsity and variable quality of available training data, the context dependence of GPCR signaling, and, importantly, the fact that network-and AI-guided polypharmacology does not yet constitute a validated or generalizable framework for designing multi-receptor interventions. Several further considerations may help define what will be required to move this exciting concept from a compelling systems-level hypothesis toward an experimentally testable and ultimately translatable framework for GPCR network pharmacology.The proposed networks contain many receptors with established disease relevance, but deciding that a receptor belongs in an aging network does not tell us how it should be modulated. A therapeutic network requires knowing whether a receptor should be activated, inhibited, partially activated, allosterically modulated, biased toward one effector, or manipulated in a tissue-restricted manner, and by how much. This distinction matters because GPCR effects are strongly dependent on receptor density, coupling repertoire, accessory proteins, cellular state, ligand concentration, and tissue context.Especially problematic is the situation for biased ligands. Compared with binding data, efficacy data are sparse and functional measurements are not interchangeable across assays.A ligand that appears biased in one cellular background may not retain the same functional preference in another because receptor expression levels, membrane lipid composition, expression reserve, transducer abundance, signal amplification, and regulatory machinery differ. Consequently, pooling efficacy measurements from heterogenous assays may obscure the underlying pharmacology and limit the predictive utility of models trained on such data.The challenge, therefore, is not simply to assemble more data, but to assemble the right data, including their experimental context.The proposed GPCRome is necessarily constrained by measurements reported in the literature. This creates an important circularity: well-studied receptors become highly connected nodes, while poorly characterized receptors, including orphan receptors (i.e., receptors without known endogenous or synthetic ligands) or incompletely deorphanized GPCRs, may be absent or misrepresented despite mediating potentially important biology, leaving major blind spots in any GPCRome network reconstruction. Boeringer et al. also highlight receptors for which human or translational evidence remains limited, with several proposed nodes supported primarily by in vitro cellular assays and animal models. It remains uncertain whether network topologies derived from controlled rodent experiments will reproduce the networks operating in complex, heterogeneous human populations.A useful next step would therefore be a community-wide effort to construct a standardized, machine-readable GPCR functional atlas. But the harder question is what such an atlas should actually measure, as binding affinity alone is insufficient. Harmonized measurements of ligand association and dissociation, receptor expression and activation, G-protein coupling, β-arrestin engagement, pathway-specific efficacy, receptor trafficking and internalization, desensitization, and signaling duration, are urgently needed-ideally across multiple physiologically relevant cellular backgrounds. Rather than reducing heterogeneous experiments to a single activity label, negative results and experimental metadata should be collected as well, and ideally shared in standardized, accessible format. Such a resource could make network inference more robust and, importantly, reveal where uncertainty really lies. While ligands reshape populations of GPCR conformations, different transducers both select receptor states and undergo their own conformational changes. Thus, signaling cannot be reduced to a ligand-induced receptor state. Rather, AI-based structure prediction, molecular dynamics and enhanced sampling, structural biology, and biophysical measurements should be considered complementary approaches for characterizing receptor-transducer conformational ensembles (Wootten et al., 2013;Hilger et al., 2018).Kinetics adds another critical dimension. Ligand residence time, receptor activation and deactivation rates, trafficking and recycling, and the duration of downstream signaling may influence in vivo efficacy and therapeutic window beyond what is captured by equilibrium affinity or endpoint efficacy (Copeland et al., 2006). Incorporating these temporal features into network models could improve both the selection of network-level interventions and the prediction of physiological outcomes.Sparse data should not necessarily halt progress, but they should change the modeling strategy. Transfer learning offers a particularly attractive route: models can learn shared representations from data-rich GPCRs and then adapt to understudied receptors, provided that domain differences and uncertainty are explicitly modeled [e.g., (Provasi and Filizola, 2025)]. The goal should not be to manufacture confidence from sparse data, but to quantify uncertainty and use it to prioritize the next experiment. AI can then become an activelearning engine linking prediction to targeted measurements rather than a one-way generator of hypotheses (Nguyen et al., 2024).A related issue is chemical space. Much of the historical GPCR ligand repertoire was optimized for individual targets, not for deliberately engineered polypharmacology. The chemical matter already available to the field may therefore be a poor representation of the multitarget molecules needed for network control. While generative modeling architectures have successfully enabled the exploration of new regions of chemical space, the objective should be defined in terms of multi-receptor and multi-pathway pharmacology, including selectivity, efficacy, kinetics, tissue exposure, and safety, rather than simply potency at one receptor. This is where structure-based methods, functional profiling, generative chemistry, and experimental validation need to be tightly coupled.Perhaps the most important question is whether the proposed network architecture will have translational relevance. Boeringer et al. (Boeringer et al. 2026) present mechanistic hypotheses that draw largely on cellular studies, animal models, and selected examples of clinical pharmacology. However, networks inferred from preclinical systems may look quite different in patients, where age, genotype, comorbidities, medication history, tissue composition, and disease stage can all reshape signaling. The authors' vision of digital twins and patient-specific GPCR interventions is compelling precisely because it points to this missing layer.The next step should be to test these network hypotheses directly against patient-derived data rather than assume that preclinical networks represent stable therapeutic maps. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, functional biomarkers, clinical phenotypes, and longitudinal treatment-response data could help establish which receptor nodes are conserved in humans and which are specific to particular tissues. Ultimately, the goal should not be to build a larger GPCR network, but a better-calibrated one that makes predictions that can be rigorously tested, challenged, and ultimately falsified in patients.A major strength of the Boeringer et al. article is that it challenges the field to think beyond the single receptor. That is an important conceptual shift. The next challenge is not simply to add more receptors, but to establish the experimental and computational standards needed to make network pharmacology genuinely testable. Such a program would: combine systematic, context-rich functional measurements with patient-derived evidence; use approaches such as transfer learning and uncertainty-aware active learning to deal with sparse data; account for receptor-transducer mechanisms and signaling kinetics rather than relying on static structures alone; and integrate physics-based and data-driven approaches to connect molecular mechanisms with cellular and organismal behavior (Hendrickx et al., 2020).The central question, then, is whether we can generate the data, assays, models, and chemical tools needed to perturb these networks in a predictable way. Turning this framework into something clinically useful will require considerably more experimental grounding and validation than the current computational roadmap implies.diseases might eventually become. But moving from theoretical network diagrams to clinically useful geroprotective therapeutics will require computational models firmly grounded in experimental biophysics and human biology. No single computational or experimental approach will be sufficient. What is needed instead is an integrated framework that brings together community-generated harmonized functional data, kinetic profiling, mechanistic modeling, generative chemistry, and patient-derived evidence. The real measure Filizola, M. documents.abstract: Teachers’ occupational well-being is associated with their capacity to sustain effective teaching and support students’ academic engagement. This study aimed to determine teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement in select districts of Cagayan de Oro City Division during the School Year 2026–2027. The study described the respondents’ profiles, assessed their occupational well-being and student engagement, examined the relationships between these variables, and tested the moderating effect of the respondents’ profiles. It used a quantitative descriptive-correlational design involving two hundred and twenty (220) Grade 7 public secondary school teachers selected through universal sampling. Data were collected using a modified questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson Correlation, and multiple regression. Findings showed that job satisfaction was stronger than work-life balance, while workload stress was more pronounced than burnout. Emotional engagement emerged as the strongest dimension of students’ academic engagement. Job satisfaction and work-life balance were significantly related to student engagement. Workload stress showed no significant relationship, while burnout had a weak link only to emotional engagement. Class size and teaching experience affected these relationships, but the subject taught did not. The study concludes that teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement are interconnected, although their relationships vary across specific dimensions and profile characteristics. School administrators and teachers are encouraged to strengthen work-life balance, manage workload stress and burnout, promote cognitive engagement, and provide support responsive to class size and teaching experience.

Three-dimensional finite element analysis in geotechnical engineering is limited by two costs, the hours a direct solver spends factorising the stiffness matrix of a fine mesh and the hours an engineer spends building the model through a graphical interface. This paper presents Tellus3D, a geotechnical finite element program that attacks both costs together by treating a large language model (LLM) agent as its primary user and a rented graphics processing unit (GPU) as its primary solver, while the engineer’s role moves from operating the program to checking what the agent did. The program exposes 31 typed tools through the Model Context Protocol, so an agent builds the soil profile, structures, tunnels and construction phases, calculates, reads the results and writes a PDF report without a graphical interface, and the same project files open in a desktop application for review. The solver uses 10-node tetrahedra with Mohr–Coulomb, Hardening Soil, HS small and Soft Soil Creep models, an effective-stress undrained formulation, fully coupled Biot consolidation with Taylor–Hood elements, embedded piles, shells with zero-thickness interface elements, vertical drains with vacuum preloading, and staged tunnel boring machine (TBM) excavation with shield contraction. Its factorisation runs on an NVIDIA GPU through cuDSS in double precision, with a supernodal multifrontal Cholesky and a quasi-definite LDLT factorisation as the CPU fallback. On an RTX 4090 the factorisation of a 275,520-equation consolidation model took 3.7 s against 237–248 s on 25 CPU cores, which is a 64-fold speed- up, and the whole ten-year embankment analysis of 13 phases finished in 14.4 min, about 19 times faster than the estimated CPU time, because the stress updates remain on the CPU. A staged 6.6 m earth pressure balance tunnel drive of 17 phases in Bangkok clay solved in 225 s. Five instrumented case histories, calculated on an RTX 5090 in 2–15 min each with up to 918,914 equations, test the predictions: the model reproduces the 36 mm wall deflection of a 21 m Bangkok excavation within 4%, the trough of twin EPB tunnels after calibrating the shield contraction, and the final settlement of a vacuum-PVD trial at Suvarnabhumi within 7%, while it settles that trial too fast in the first six weeks, fails the Muar embankment about 1 m below the measured failure height, and moves a river wall of cement-admixed clay columns in stiff clay by about 6 mm against 42.6 mm measured. The analyses ran on a rented GPU costing about US$0.4 per hour, and the paper reports the verification and field benchmarks, the limits that the engineer must check, and why the remaining CPU work now bounds the speed-up.

The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Visual perception is often studied through the lens of object recognition. However, a large fraction of visual experience concerns image properties that are not naturally described in terms of discrete objects or categories. Visual textures provide a useful method to investigate this complementary aspect of vision, as they can be described through image statistics while spanning a wide range of perceptual and semantic complexity. In this thesis, I investigate how textures are represented in deep neural networks and humans, combining texture synthesis, representation analysis, computational modeling, and psychophysics. I first explored whether the naturalistic texture representations introduced by Gatys et al. (2015) could be combined with the latent space of a Variational Autoencoder to construct a controllable generative model of naturalistic textures. Although the complete model did not achieve the intended performance, the experiments isolated the texture representation proposed by Gatys as the most robust component of our framework and motivated a direct investigation of its representational properties. I then studied texture representations coded as Gram matrices across a diverse set of convolutional neural networks trained for object recognition. Texture information increased with network depth, but the resulting representations recovered only part of the categorical structure of natural textures defined by human judgment. Crucially, their quality was not correlated with measures of neural or behavioral alignment in object recognition. This dissociation indicates that being a good model of the ventral visual stream in an object recognition setting does not necessarily imply representing textures in a human-like way. Finally, I extended this analysis beyond convolutional architectures by comparing one CNN with three Vision Transformers across textures of progressively increasing complexity and with human performance in a psychophysical discrimination task. Vision Transformers formed substantially more consistent representations across texture types than the CNN, and these representational relationships were significantly better aligned with human perception. Taken together, these results show that texture perception provides a complementary benchmark for computational models of vision and exposes limitations within the dominant object recognition paradigm. More broadly, I suggest that understanding biological visual representations requires models and evaluation criteria that account not only for object identity and semantic content, but also for the statistical and contextual structure through which visual appearance is organized.

Purpose This study examined how speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety relate to second or foreign language (L2) learners’ willingness to communicate (WTC) in a GenAI-enhanced learning environment. More specifically, the study focused on the joint associations of these psycho-emotional variables with WTC and examined whether their alignment or discrepancy was related to learners’ communication willingness.Methodology A sample of 280 L2 learners completed measures of speaking self-efficacy, speaking anxiety, and WTC within a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enhanced learning environment. Bivariate correlations were first examined to establish the associations among the variables. Response surface analysis (RSA) was then employed to examine the joint associations of speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety with WTC.Findings Speaking self-efficacy was positively associated with WTC, whereas speaking anxiety was negatively associated with WTC. The significant interaction between speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety indicated that their associations with WTC varied as a function of each other. The RSA showed that the direction of incongruence between speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety was systematically associated with WTC, with WTC higher when the discrepancy favored greater self-efficacy and lower anxiety. At the configuration level, the incongruent combination of high speaking self-efficacy and low speaking anxiety was associated with the highest WTC.Originality/value The study extends research on L2 learners’ WTC by moving beyond separate examinations of speaking self-efficacy and speaking anxiety and considering how these experiences operate in combination within a GenAI-enhanced instructional context.

The AI Courtroom: How Artificial Intelligence Is Reshaping Legal Practice explores the transformative role of artificial intelligence in the legal profession and the judicial system. The book examines how AI technologies are changing legal research, case analysis, contract drafting, evidence evaluation, litigation strategies, and courtroom administration. It highlights the opportunities offered by automation, predictive analytics, machine learning, and generative AI in improving efficiency, accuracy, and access to justice. At the same time, it critically addresses challenges related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, professional ethics, and the reliability of AI-generated legal information. The book also explores the evolving responsibilities of judges, lawyers, law firms, and legal institutions in an increasingly technology-driven environment. By connecting technological innovation with legal principles and judicial accountability, it provides valuable insights for law students, researchers, legal practitioners, policymakers, and technology professionals. Ultimately, the book emphasizes the importance of adopting AI responsibly while preserving human judgment, fairness, and the fundamental principles of justice.

Last month, leading executives of artificial intelligence (AI) companies warned the United Nations Security Council about the risks of losing human control over this rapidly advancing technology. Their recommendations focused heavily on safeguards, evaluation, and governance of AI models and systems, largely overlooking the risks that arise from the interactions of AI with people and institutions. AI safety needs to be addressed at the level of the human–AI system, not the AI model alone.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Drawing from critical theoretical and empirical research, this study situates the Brussels Effect in HRM by problematising the processes of the globalisation of algorithmic workload management as a “regulatory mirage” of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act with its extraterritorial reach. The Act requires that high-risk HR systems be managed for risk, have human oversight, and be transparent; however, it does not provide for substantive worker dignity. The analysis shows a two-tiered global labour market based on the geography of the employer, with Global South workers at a disadvantage. The proposal made in this study is a Model Global Human Resource Artificial Intelligence Governance Protocol to bring the procedures into agreement with ethical justice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Capture-the-flag (CTF) competitions are used across the security community to recruit talent, build skills and sustain a competitive culture. As AI agents increasingly solve CTF challenges, three positions have emerged: that the format is obsolete, that it should become a benchmark for human-AI collaboration, and that headline claims overstate what the saturation of introductory benchmarks shows. This debate has been driven mainly by capability benchmarks, while the views of those who design, run and play CTFs remain largely unexamined. We report an exploratory qualitative study based on six interviews (seven participants) and eleven anonymous written responses from experienced CTF organisers and players. We interpret their accounts using Bourdieu's concepts of field and capital, and, for learning, the notion of threshold concepts. Participants did not offer a single verdict. Some were strongly critical of AI-assisted solving in competition; others wanted AI to be embraced and built into CTFs; still others took positions that depended on context. Strongly critical positions were voiced more often in anonymous written responses, a reminder that such positions are situated in the circumstances in which accounts are given. Participants involved in competition-focused CTFs described rankings that increasingly reflect access to AI models and money, and a loss of the satisfaction that made competing worthwhile. From an educational perspective, participants described students who solved challenges quickly but could not explain how they had done so. Participants disagreed about whether CTFs are preparation for real-world practice or a sport, and this seemed closely related to the stance they took. Many saw the enforcement of anti-AI measures as feasible only in on-site CTFs, and also largely dependent on trust. Several participants expressed doubt about CTF results still signalling individual skill levels to potential employers. We propose that this exploratory study into CTFs indicates a wider problem for the security workforce: when a measure of skill becomes cheap and easy to automate, a community must renegotiate what counts as legitimate performance. We also discuss implications for skills development, competition governance and hiring.

35.2% of task time in world employment is at least partly delegable to AI agents in 2026, and only 2.5% can be handed over in full. Existing measures score exposure to generative AI, mostly for the United States. We build the Agent Delegability Index (ADI): two language models rate all 18,796 O*NET 30.2 task statements on a frozen, preregistered rubric of delegation levels and barriers; tasks are mapped to 433 ISCO-08 unit groups and weighted by ILOSTAT employment in 146 countries. Four findings. First, delegable employment rises with income, from 22.5% in low-income to 48.7% in high-income countries, a slope of 7.23 percentage points per log point of GDP per capita. This delegation divide is compositional: the physical barrier dominates the jobs poorer countries employ most. Second, at the occupation level ADI tracks exposure closely (r = 0.93 with Eloundou et al. and 0.89 with Felten et al.), above the preregistered bound of 0.80; ADI adds delegation levels and barriers on top of exposure, for the world, not a new ranking of occupations. Third, full delegation is rare and peaks for tasks that take a human about twelve minutes (11.8 minutes). Fourth, the preregistered adoption gap is not supported: across 101 countries, delegability and observed AI usage correlate at r = 0.86, and the gap between them is not wider in middle-income countries (p = 0.27). Model agreement is kappa = 0.77; a blind human rating of 300 tasks agrees with the model consensus at kappa = 0.85, and an agentic panel with web search at kappa = 0.87. We release the index, the atlas, the prompts and an MCP server at https://github.com/Cespial/delegation-divide.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: The Digital Double Traffic Light is a global policy proposal advocating a legally mandatory transparency label for commercial digital services, including social media, streaming, gaming and artificial intelligence. The proposal introduces two simple consumer indicators: A revenue indicator showing the average revenue generated by a digital provider from user activity. An environmental indicator estimating the electricity, water consumption and CO₂ emissions associated with digital use. The initiative calls for mandatory disclosure of aggregated, independently verifiable data, while protecting personal privacy and allowing proportionate requirements for smaller providers. Its goal is to promote informed consumer choice, digital transparency and responsible resource use without restricting individual freedom. This concept paper is provided in German, English and Simplified Chinese. Initiator and author: Gerd Kühnen, Germany, October 2026.

Oncology nurses face high rates of psychosocial strain and musculoskeletal disorders that reinforce one another, yet ACT-based interventions targeting this population remain scarce, particularly in Iran. This quasi-experimental before-after study examined the effect of a six-session Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) program on burnout and musculoskeletal discomfort among 40 oncology nurses at a hospital in Kerman, Iran, selected by census sampling. Burnout was measured with the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory and musculoskeletal discomfort with the Localized Postural Discomfort scale before and after the intervention, with data analyzed using paired t-tests and repeated-measures ANCOVA. Following the intervention, overall burnout decreased significantly ( P < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.78), driven by reductions in work- and patient-related burnout, while personal burnout remained unchanged. Discomfort in the neck, low back, and shoulders also decreased significantly ( P < 0.05). These findings support ACT-based training as a low-cost, evidence-based strategy for improving oncology nurses' occupational health and patient care quality.

This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in improving students’ critical reading skills in higher education. As digital technologies increasingly shape learning environments, AI offers potential to enhance higher-order thinking. This research employed a quantitative approach using a quasi-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design. The participants were 30 sixth-semester students enrolled in the Qualitative Research on ELT course at Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa, selected through purposive sampling. The instrument was a standardized critical reading test measuring students’ ability to identify main ideas, analyze arguments, evaluate evidence, detect bias, and draw conclusions. It included multiple-choice and short-response items to assess analytical comprehension. The treatment integrated AI-based tools for text analysis, summarization, argument mapping, and reflective questioning. Students also compared their interpretations with AI-generated feedback to enhance metacognitive awareness. The intervention was conducted over four meetings under guided supervision. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and a paired-sample t-test. The findings revealed a statistically significant improvement in students’ posttest scores compared to pretest results at the 0.05 level. These results indicate that AI can effectively support critical reading development and foster deeper engagement with academic texts in EFL contexts.

This study examines the effects of transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards on job performance, with affective commitment serving as a mediating variable, in Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia. Public sector organizations face increasing demands to improve performance while maintaining bureaucratic accountability and regulatory compliance. Understanding the mechanisms that influence performance in such institutional settings is therefore essential. A quantitative explanatory approach was employed using survey data collected from 311 civil servants. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results show that transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards positively and significantly influence job performance. Both variables also have significant positive effects on affective commitment, which in turn enhances job performance. Furthermore, affective commitment partially mediates the relationships between transformational leadership, intrinsic rewards, and job performance. These findings highlight the importance of leadership practices and intrinsic motivational factors in strengthening employee commitment and improving performance in public sector institutions. The study provides empirical evidence from Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia and offers practical implications for performance management in bureaucratic contexts.

Abstract The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic writing raises questions about authorship, reflexivity, and epistemic responsibility in social work scholarship. This study examines whether generative AI can reproduce not only the structural features of scholarly discourse but also the reflexive and contextually embedded knowledge practices central to critical social work. A qualitative comparative case design was employed, comparing a human-authored article on multicultural social work (2010, Turkish context) with an AI-generated text produced under controlled conditions using identical references and thematic structure. Analysis focused on three dimensions: theoretical integration, reflexivity and epistemic positioning, and contextual embeddedness. While the AI-generated text demonstrated strong structural coherence and citation alignment, differences emerged in dialectical engagement, explicit normative positioning, and national contextual grounding. The findings suggest that generative AI can simulate disciplinary discourse but does not inherently enact accountable epistemic agency, underscoring the continuing importance of reflexive human authorship.

documents.abstract: The flipped classroom (FC) model has obtained collective attention in medical education for its potential to enhance student engagement, active learning, and knowledge retention.This study systematically reviews the report on flipped classrooms in medical education using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta- Analyses (PRISMA) framework. Articles were retrieved from reputable databases, including PubMed, Medline, OVID, ACM, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, MDPI, SAGE, SpringerLink, Wiley, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar.The 34 studies were identified exploring flipped classroom teaching approaches to enhance medical education. Review focuses on the tools and technologies employed such as video creation, learning management systems, podcasts, online assessments, and collaborative platforms as well as pedagogical strategies implemented across medical courses.This study focused on flipped learning in higher education. Future research should examine its application in other educational settings, including schools, vocational, technical, and professional training. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and augmented reality warrant investigation for their impact on student engagement and learning outcomes across disciplines. Further studies should also explore the influence of cultural and geographical factors on flipped classroom implementation and effectiveness. Additionally, research is needed to determine how flipped classroom activities can be tailored to specific learning objectives, student needs, and subject areas. Finally, longitudinal studies are recommended to assess the long- term effects of flipped learning on student achievement, retention, and academic success.

Metaphor is a crucial aspect of human cognition. As such, we would like to understand how it is represented in large language models (LLMs) and how it might be controlled. We use mechanistic interpretability techniques to identify causal subspaces in a range of LLMs covering different architectures and sizes. We show that we are able to steer output on classification tasks across different parts of speech. We are also able to steer output on generation tasks, indicating that these techniques can be used to control the metaphoricity of LLM output.

• Age-related disruption of GPCR networks may connect inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, and other hallmarks of aging through shared signaling mechanisms.• Network-level GPCR targeting could move geroscience beyond single-receptor pharmacology toward coordinated, multisystem interventions tailored to aging biology.• AI, multiomics, and digital-twin approaches may enable more precise GPCR-based therapies, but their clinical value will depend on high-quality data, rigorous validation, and overcoming major translational and regulatory barriers.We are living in an era of remarkable global demographic shifts, with most people now expected to live into their seventies and many well beyond. However, this extension of lifespan has also highlighted a persistent gap in "healthspan"-the period of life spent free from chronic, debilitating conditions. Advanced age remains the primary risk factor for a broad spectrum of illnesses, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, and cancer. Because the care and treatment of people with these conditions and their comorbidities places an unsustainable strain on healthcare systems, the field of geroscience seeks to target the shared biological root causes of aging itself (1,2).Early therapeutic strategies in this space focused heavily on "senolytics"-compounds engineered to selectively eliminate senescent cells. However, translating senolytic agents from preclinical models to human patients has proven difficult. Because senescent cells share many internal survival pathways with healthy cells in vital tissues, first-generation senolytic approaches have raised concerns about significant systemic adverse effects, including blood disorders or impaired wound healing. These translational hurdles underline the ongoing need for therapeutic strategies with improved tissue selectivity and safety profiles.In their lead article, Boeringer et al. advocate for a systematic focus on the cell surface, specifically targeting G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (1). The largest family of transmembrane proteins in the human genome, GPCRs modulate a wide range of hormonal, metabolic, neural, and immunological processes, many of which tend to undergo dysregulation with age (1,3). Because of their accessibility on the surfaces of virtually every cell, and their vital roles in endocrine, paracrine, and autocrine signaling, GPCRs are already the targets of more than one-third of current pharmacotherapeutics approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration.The authors build their case on a biological convergence across the five major, structurally distinct families: Class A (rhodopsin-like), Class B1 (secretin-like), Class B2 (adhesion), Class C (glutamate), and Class F (Frizzled/Smoothened) (1). Despite their notable structural differences, all five GPCR families show age-related changes in expression, trafficking, or signaling that can disrupt receptor function (1). Human physiological aging is associated with reductions in plasma membrane levels, increased internalization, and reduced heterotrimeric G protein coupling in Class A and Class B1 receptors, as well as defective mechanotransduction and altered dimer stability in Class B2 and Class C families (1). Class F receptors also display an age-related loss of homeostatic tone driven by increased levels of soluble functional antagonists. This convergence of age-related decay of signaling fidelity suggests that aging may act through shared downstream mechanisms, such as molecular chaperone dysfunction, lysosomal decay, and altered lipid raft composition, positioning the GPCR-ome as a deeply interconnected network (1). To understand how this network misfires over time, we must first map the physical and functional architecture that links these families together. Our laboratory has focused on decoding this underlying structural complexity, using multiplexed mapping strategies to systematically chart the functional interactome of GPCRs alongside their critical receptor activity-modifying accessory networks (4). This system-wide interconnectivity underpins Boeringer et al.'s argument that the GPCR-ome behaves as a deeply integrated molecular switchboard (1), providing a rational basis for moving beyond traditional single-receptor pharmacology toward a broader, network-level strategy for rebalancing cellular signaling in aging.One of the most practical applications of this cell-surface framework is the modulation of the cellular secretome, particularly the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).Senescent cells drive localized tissue damage by developing a SASP and secreting a complex mixture of proinflammatory cytokines, growth factors, and proteases that promote chronic inflammation and drive age-related pathologies across multiple organs (2).The lead article maps how chronic perturbations in specific Class A receptors are linked to systemic and progressive "inflammaging" (1). Specifically, age-associated increases in chemokine receptors, including C-X-C chemokine receptors 2 and 4 (CXCR2/4) and C-C chemokine receptors 2 and 5 (CCR2/5), directly fuel persistent leukocyte activation and chronic inflammation. In this context, the authors highlight the potential of senomorphics to counteract some of these changes using small-molecule therapeutics to modulate or suppress specific hyperactive surface receptors, which in turn may modify or block the production of toxic SASP factors without killing the cell outright (1). Identifying and targeting GPCR pairings that regulate specific proinflammatory interleukins could interrupt the localized inflammatory cascade, thereby protecting surrounding tissues and organs.An important tension in geroscience is the dual role of cellular senescence. Senescence serves as a vital biological defense against oncogenesis, forcing severely damaged or mutated cells into permanent cell-cycle arrest to act as an emergency tumor brake. Consequently, broad or uncritical ablation of senescent cells carries the risk of removing beneficial tumor-suppressive functions of senescence and potentially increasing a patient's vulnerability to cancer. Conversely, leaving senescent cells completely unchecked allows chronic SASP secretions to steadily degrade the surrounding extracellular matrix, creating a microenvironment for tumors to grow, escape immune detection, and metastasize.Our work exploring the intersection of these signaling pathways has shown that specific receptor complexes can modulate both proliferation and senescence entry, depending on how they are engaged (5). Boeringer et al. propose GPCR-targeted interventions as a potential therapeutic strategy because these receptors communicate through highly specific, multilayered downstream pathways that are amenable to fine-tuned pharmacological regulation (1). For example, "biased" GPCR ligands can, in principle, be engineered to alter selected receptor conformations to engage beneficial signaling pathways while minimizing off-target effects. In this context, biased ligands could induce a cell to shut down its cancer-promoting inflammatory secretions while leaving its internal, tumor-suppressing cell-cycle arrest mechanisms intact. Furthermore, distinct surface expression profiles and unique structural patterns that arise on aged cells could act as precise molecular docking stations (6,7) to allow longevity researchers to guide antibody-drug conjugates or smart nanoparticles directly to target cells.Boeringer et al. successfully contextualize the broader systemic impact of GPCR networks by examining metabolic health and neurodegeneration as examples (1). In metabolic regulation, receptors responsive to incretin hormones, such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor (GLP-1R), undergo age-related declines in responsiveness that impair insulin sensitivity, disrupt glucose handling, and contribute to type 2 diabetes. Conversely, the Class B1 glucagon receptor (GCGR) exhibits pathological hypersensitivity in the liver with age, accelerating hepatic steatosis and driving the mitochondrial overload and insulin resistance seen in metabolic syndrome. Restoring nutrient homeostasis and targeting downstream cell-surface pathways show immense promise in rescuing β-cell function, maintaining cellular proliferation, and protecting vasculature from hyperglycemia-induced senescence (8)(9)(10). Medicines with multi-incretin agonist activity that optimize these cell-surface networks show promise in restoring proper nutrient sensing and activating downstream protective pathways.For neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, Class A, Class B2, and Class C receptors are known to modulate pathological mechanisms, including neuroinflammation, excitotoxicity, and synaptic plasticity. The authors highlight a striking metric: large-scale genetic analyses have identified 22 specific GPCRs with direct links to Alzheimer's traits, yet fewer than 15% of these genetically identified targets are actively being explored in current clinical trials (3). This statistic serves as a clarion call that current pharmaceutical drug development pipelines may not be ideally suited to developing drugs for heterogeneous or multisystem disorders. Rather than aggressively responding to robust genetic population data, the current drug-discovery infrastructure remains anchored to legacy targets, leaving a vast, highly accessible reservoir of brain-specific receptors largely unexploited.While the conceptual framework linking the GPCR-ome to the hallmarks of aging is compelling, it is crucial to distinguish genuine data-driven insights from predictions generated by artificial intelligence (AI). Boeringer et al. outline a forward-looking technological roadmap that integrates AI for state-specific structural modeling, quantum computing for atomic-precision docking simulations, and multiomics data integration to build patient-specific "digital twins."While it is certainly likely that next-generation medicine will integrate many of these tools to improve healthcare outcomes, stubborn translational bottlenecks are hampering current progress.Simulating an entire human multireceptor signaling network via quantum machine learning that might influence healthcare practice remains an interesting but currently hypothetical exercise. As the authors acknowledge, these advanced deep learning models operate as "black boxes" that are limited by the quality, scope, and curation of human-derived training data, which remain sparse, heavily fragmented, and poorly standardized across the academic literature. Furthermore, designing multireceptor interventions is notoriously difficult due to the inherent promiscuity and pleiotropic nature of GPCR signaling systems. Translating a theoretically perfect AI-generated drug network into a safe, nontoxic, and stable polypharmacological regimen might require years of empirical validation, iterative preclinical testing, and resolution of massive regulatory hurdles regarding composite healthspan endpoints (1).In summary, Boeringer et al. provide a highly useful synthesis of how cell-surface signaling interfaces with the complex, multisystemic processes of aging. By framing age-related health decline as part of a larger, systemic drift in GPCR network balance at the cellular level-where hyperactivation of pro-aging receptors coexists with hypoactivation of pro-longevity receptorsthe authors offer a cohesive perspective that connects disparate fields of aging research.While a universal therapeutic solution remains aspirational, evaluating the GPCR-ome as an integrated molecular switchboard provides geroscience with a structured, data-driven approach to systems pharmacology (1). The lead article's computational pathways provide a useful roadmap for long-term future investigation. Ultimately, continued interdisciplinary investment in mapping the cell-surface landscape of the GPCR-ome will be essential to determine whether these network-level strategies can be translated to clinical applications with the aim of extending human healthspan.

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Endoscopy is central to gastrointestinal care but is associated with significant occupational stressors, including high workload, physical strain, and psychological impact following complications. Data on endoscopist wellbeing in the Middle East remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence of burnout, musculoskeletal symptoms, and emotional consequences of complications among endoscopists in Saudi Arabia. METHODS: A national cross-sectional survey was conducted between October and November 2025 among licensed endoscopists across Saudi Arabia. The questionnaire assessed demographic characteristics, workload, musculoskeletal symptoms, burnout indicators, complication experience, emotional impact, and institutional support. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. RESULTS: A total of 76 endoscopists participated. High workload was common, with 73.7% performing ≥20 procedures per week and 78.9% working ≥41 hours weekly. Musculoskeletal symptoms were reported by 64.5% (49/76). Burnout-related indicators included frequent fatigue (28.9%) and emotional exhaustion (17.1%). Working ≥41 hours per week was independently associated with frequent fatigue. A significant complication was reported by 64.5%, with psychological effects including sleep disturbance (56.6%), intrusive thoughts (27.6%), and loss of confidence (35.5%). Avoidance of similar procedures occurred in 35.5%, while 60.5% reported no formal debriefing or institutional support. CONCLUSION: Endoscopists in Saudi Arabia experience a substantial physical and psychological burden, compounded by limited institutional support. Targeted interventions, including ergonomic training, structured debriefing, and peer-support programs, are needed to improve clinician wellbeing and sustain endoscopy services.

documents.abstract: Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into specialized translation workflows introduces nuanced lexical and register-related challenges. This exploratory case study investigates how progressively constrained prompt engineering influences the translation of domain-specific pedagogical terminology from English into Arabic. Using ChatGPT Pro (GPT-4), an 84-word source excerpt containing four key Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT) pedagogical terms was translated under three prompting conditions: zero-shot baseline, role-prompting (expert persona), and context-rich prompting (localized to Moroccan secondary education). The resulting Arabic outputs were evaluated against recognized Moroccan pedagogical frameworks and specialized Arabic educational lexicons using an explicit three-tier adequacy rubric. Descriptive analysis revealed marked lexical variations: zero-shot prompting yielded literal semantic calques, whereas context-rich prompting aligned closely with localized curricular terminology. While these exploratory findings demonstrate that contextual constraints assist the model in selecting domain-appropriate registers, the results highlight the necessity of continued human expertise and institutional oversight in specialized machine translation post-editing.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered technologies are increasingly being employed to help EFL students with academic writing. However, research into the combined use of DeepL and QuillBot during the writing process is sparse. This study looks on students' use and perceptions of DeepL and QuillBot in academic writing. Using a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were gathered from 49 English Education students through a 35-item five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with nine participants and analysed thematically. The data revealed that both instruments were generally viewed positively. DeepL was mostly utilized for translation and phrase improvement during planning and drafting, while QuillBot helped with paraphrasing and editing. Students did not rely solely on AI results; rather, they critically analyzed and corrected generated texts. The study finds that DeepL and QuillBot serve as supportive tools that improve academic writing while allowing students to retain control over content and meaning.

The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, has transformed learning practices in higher education while raising concerns about student dependency and academic integrity. Although previous studies have primarily examined the effects of AI usage intensity, limited attention has been given to how institutional policies shape AI utilization and subsequently influence dependency. This study addresses this gap by examining the effects of ChatGPT usage level and institutional policies on student dependency, with ChatGPT utilization as a mediating variable. A quantitative approach was employed involving 113 students from Politeknik Ilmu Pelayaran Semarang, Indonesia, selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 3. The findings indicate that institutional policies significantly enhance ChatGPT utilization but do not directly affect dependency. In contrast, ChatGPT utilization has a significant negative effect on dependency, suggesting that higher-quality utilization reduces the likelihood of excessive reliance. The level of ChatGPT usage does not significantly influence either utilization or dependency. Furthermore, ChatGPT utilization fully mediates the relationship between institutional policies and dependency. These findings extend the literature on AI adoption and technology dependency by demonstrating that the quality of AI utilization, rather than usage intensity, is the primary mechanism through which institutional policies influence dependency. This study suggests a shift from frequency-based perspectives toward utilization-oriented approaches in understanding responsible AI adoption in higher education. Practically, higher education institutions should prioritize policies that promote AI literacy, establish clear ethical guidelines, integrate ChatGPT into learning activities with appropriate supervision, and encourage reflective rather than passive AI use to maximize educational benefits while minimizing dependency.

documents.abstract: Mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and learning engagement are central to children's mathematics learning, yet their longitudinal interplay remains insufficiently understood. This study examined dynamic associations among these constructs by following 3354 Chinese third- to fifth-grade students across three waves: December 2024, June 2025, and December 2025. To capture dimension-specific processes, six random-intercept cross-lagged panel models were estimated by crossing two dimensions of mathematics anxiety (learning and evaluation) with three dimensions of learning engagement (behavioral, cognitive, and emotional). Results indicated that within-person increases in mathematics learning and evaluation anxiety were prospectively associated with decreases in subsequent academic grit and learning engagement across dimensions. Within-person increases in behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement generally predicted lower subsequent mathematics anxiety and higher academic grit. Academic grit showed reciprocal associations with mathematics anxiety and indirectly linked mathematics anxiety to subsequent behavioral engagement; however, corresponding indirect effects involving cognitive and emotional engagement were less consistent. Educational relevance and implications statement This study followed Chinese upper elementary school children over one year to understand how mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and mathematics learning engagement develop together. The findings showed that when children experienced higher levels of mathematics anxiety, whether during learning or evaluation, they tended to show lower subsequent academic grit and lower behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement in mathematics. In turn, greater engagement was followed by greater academic grit and lower mathematics anxiety. Moreover, behavioral, cognitive and emotional learning engagement were indirectly associated with lower subsequent mathematics evaluation anxiety through academic grit. These findings suggest that, in mathematics education, encouraging children to “try harder” or exert greater behavioral effort in mathematics is valuable but may not be sufficient. Teachers should also carefully design instructional materials and learning activities that foster children's emotional and cognitive engagement in mathematics. Such efforts may support the development of academic grit and potentially contribute to reducing mathematics anxiety, particularly in evaluation situations.

This chapter aims to examine the role played by artificial intelligence in determining the consumer behaviors and buying patterns of children in a digital environment. The chapter focuses on the mechanisms employed by artificial intelligence in marketing, which include collecting consumer data, tracking consumer behavior, persuasion architecture, artificial influencers, hyper-personalization, the Internet of Toys, and voice assistants. The chapter is also concerned with the psychological and emotional triggers employed by artificial intelligence in marketing to consumers, which include fear of missing out, gamification, and reward-based engagement systems. The chapter is concerned with the ethical issues associated with artificial intelligence marketing to consumers, which include issues related to consumer data privacy, manipulation, transparency, and the lack of regulations. The chapter is also concerned with emerging trends in artificial intelligence marketing to consumers, which include considerations related to marketing ethics

documents.abstract: This technical deposit provides empirical evidence that state-of-the-art AI video generation models (including architectures from Runway, Luma, OpenAI, and Google) do not merely render aesthetic pixels. They function as implicit topological solvers and latent physicists. To test this, we subjected these models to a rigorous, closed-loop formal logic stress test using the invariants of a deterministic biophysical framework (the V3 Architecture). The AI was forced to solve for strict mathematical and geometric constraints, including volumetric density, scale factor, master frequency, surface coherence density, heptadic closure, and a critical failure threshold. === THE EXPERIMENTAL REVELATION === When the native constraints were injected into the AI (Sequence A), the generative engine output a perfectly fluid, harmoniously coupled micrometric network, reflecting structural stability and physical consistency. However, when a single specific mathematical constant was deliberately violated (Sequence B)—such as breaking the topological 7-fold closure or shifting the critical potential threshold—the AI video engine did not exhibit random noise or visual hallucination. Instead, it triggered an immediate, precise cascade of structural decoherence, geometric twisting, and spatial collapse across the intracellular matrix. === IMPLICATIONS FOR AI ARCHITECTURE === This experiment proves that large-scale generative diffusion models implicitly capture deep physical dependencies and mathematical rules within their latent spaces. documents.abstract: Generative AI policies often center on whether tools should be permitted, restricted, or detected, yet these questions do not address how students learn to select and evaluate academic support. This chapter introduces CLEAR—Clarify, Locate, Engage, Assess, and Revise/Reflect—an instructional cycle developed through practitioner action research in online first-year composition. Grounded in self-regulated learning, Universal Design for Learning, resource literacy, and instructor-modeled GenAI use, CLEAR positions GenAI as one optional resource within a broader support system. A comparative study included 11 matched participants across SRL-only, AI-only, and CLEAR conditions. The missing UDL-only group prevented the planned factorial analyses, while small samples and measurement limitations restrict the findings to exploratory patterns. CLEAR is therefore presented as a theoretically grounded, human-centered framework that makes resource judgment visible and teachable.

Advanced ventilation modes represent a paradigm shift in critical care through real-time physiological adaptability and smart automation. Unlike traditional ventilation strategies with fixed preset parameters and intermittent intervention, these modes use sophisticated algorithms and continuous feedback from patient respiratory mechanics and neural signals to modulate ventilatory support dynamically. Technologies like Adaptive Support Ventilation, Proportional Assist Ventilation, Neurally Adjusted Ventilatory Assist, and computerised weaning tools like SmartCare enhance synchrony between ventilator and patient, reduce the work of breathing, and enable earlier weaning. These advantages lead to improved clinical results, such as reduced mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit length of stay. There are shortcomings in the lack of control by the clinician with a quickly developing lung pathology, restricted pediatric experience, and pragmatic constraints surrounding device compatibility and instruction. This narrative review addresses how new technologies integrating oxygenation and carbon dioxide monitoring with artificial intelligence and machine learning offer the potential for better personalisation and optimisation of respiratory therapy. Additional research and development must be executed to overcome current limitations and take full advantage of these intelligent ventilation systems, which promise to make a significant difference in critical care practice and patient outcomes worldwide. Clinicians should consider these intelligent ventilation modes in appropriately selected patients to improve patient–ventilator synchrony, facilitate earlier weaning, and optimise personalised respiratory support, while remaining mindful of their limitations and the need for careful clinical oversight.

This chapter.investigates carbon-aware.computing.as.a.solution for reducing data centers' environmental impact amid surging AI-driven demand. It argues that the carbon footprint of computing depends on.timing and location of consumption, positioning carbon intensity as a critical metric. The chapter examines temporal, spatial, and alternative workload shifting, proposes a taxonomic.framework for classifying workload flexibility, and addresses the Green AI versus Red AI dilemma. It further explores predictive grid integration wherein data centers become active smart grid participants. The chapter contends that artificial intelligence is simultaneously a cause of and a solution to data center energy challenges.
